extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and policymakers interested in political economy and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing public-policy and economic actions by weighing immediate, visible consequences against delayed or hidden (unseen) effects; uses concrete examples (broken window, troops, taxes, public works, theatres) to illustrate common fallacies. Emphasises reasoning about net social welfare rather than isolated, visible impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account_for_that_which_is_seen_and_that_which_is_not_seen
rubrics_metrics.description: In the department of economy, an act, a habit, an institution, a law, gives birth not only to an effect, but to a series of effects. Of these effects, the first only is immediate; it manifests itself simultaneously with its cause--it is seen. The others unfold in succession--they are not seen: it is well for us if they are foreseen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whole difference between a good and a bad economist is that the good economist takes account both of the effects which are seen and of those which must be foreseen. The bad economist pursues a small present good that will be followed by a great evil; the true economist may risk a small present evil to pursue a great future good. Examples: broken window, disbanding troops, taxes, public works, theatres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken_window_fallacy:_destruction_is_not_profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Supposing a broken pane of glass costs six francs to repair; the glazier gains six francs (that which is seen). But it is not seen that the shopkeeper cannot spend those six francs on shoes or a book; society loses the value of the broken window. "Destruction is not profit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conclude that acts of destruction are beneficial because they 'encourage' certain trades. Always identify all parties affected (consumer, visible producer, and the unseen displaced producer) and account for the lost alternative uses of funds. Anti-pattern: praising war, fires, or other destruction on the grounds they 'create work.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public_expenditure_displaces_private_expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislature votes money for an object (e.g., 60,000 francs for theatres), it takes that money from taxpayers who would otherwise use it; the vote merely displaces enjoyments and transposes wages rather than adding to national well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that public spending 'supports the working classes' confuse displacement with net gain. To justify public spending, prove its intrinsic utility to the public (value to the taxpayer) rather than pointing to the visible beneficiaries. Example: support for theatres shifts money from other workers to artists without increasing total national labour or enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes:_visible_benefits_vs_unseen_costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantages officials advocate are those which are seen (the expense of the official and the benefit to his providers); the disadvantages the taxpayers suffer are those which are not seen (the taxpayer prevented from spending the same sum elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing taxation, do not treat the official's spending as a net gain; it is a transfer that reduces private spending elsewhere. If the official provides a truly useful service, there is no loss; otherwise taxation-funded spending can be equivalent to theft. Avoid using 'it supports labour' as a justification without demonstrating net utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public_works_create_seen_jobs_but_may_not_increase_net_employment
rubrics_metrics.description: The State opens a road, builds a palace, etc., and so gives work to certain workmen (what is seen); but it deprives other workmen of work (what is not seen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public works by comparing their social utility to the private projects they displace. Consider the source of funds (taxation) and the alternative private expenditures that are prevented. Beware the simplistic claim 'it creates labour' as justification without assessing net productive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbanding_troops_example:_productive_vs_unproductive_labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining soldiers costs money and supports consumption at garrison towns (seen). But the country pays for unproductive labour rather than productive labour; disbanding returns money to taxpayers and can convert unproductive into productive labour without net loss in total demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't judge solely by the visible immediate employment effect; consider whether labour is productive (creates value) or unproductive (consumes resources without producing) and trace how funds circulate when employment status changes. The fear that disbanding will reduce wages ignores that the funds move back into the economy as demand for labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do_not_justify_public_offices_or_luxury_by_their_stimulus_to_industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that the luxury and splendour of government officers or public banquets 'encourage the arts, industry, and labour' confuse a visible reallocation of spending with a net increase in national welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require demonstration of intrinsic public utility for expensive official trappings rather than asserting they 'attract men of merit' or 'support industry.' Apply arithmetic: transferring money from one use to another does not change the sum total of satisfactions unless the service provided equals its cost to taxpayers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State_support_of_arts_should_be_justified_by_intrinsic_utility,_not_by_employment_counts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are arguments both for and against state support of the arts; while supporters cite employment and cultural benefits, opponents point out the distributive injustice of abridging artisans' wages to add to artists' profits and that state aid may simply displace private patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess state patronage by asking whether it adds net public value and by considering distributive justice; do not accept 'it supports so many workmen' as proof of utility without comparing to what taxpayers lose. Consider whether artistic activity can flourish without State intervention (examples: London's exhibition without government support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free_exchange_harmonizes_class_interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Because men exchange their labour and productions, a harmonious tie attaches the classes one to the other: manufacturers seeking cheaper raw materials and better machines promote abundance and low prices that benefit consumers; capitalists economise and increase capital which tends to reduce interest benefiting borrowers and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge the presumption of a natural, irreconcilable antagonism between capitalists and workers. In policy evaluation, consider how individual efforts toward self-interest can produce common benefits via market processes. Anti-pattern: presuming class antagonism as an axiom when judging economic arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_judging_policies_by_immediate_visible_effects_only
rubrics_metrics.description: It is insufficient to confine judgement to immediate consequences; one must also consider the subsequent, less visible consequences. The 'seen' can be favourable while the 'not seen' fatal, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical rule, before endorsing a policy because of visible benefits, enumerate and estimate displaced alternatives and long-run effects. Use concrete counterexamples (broken window, taxes, public works, theatres, troops) to test intuitions about apparent economic benefits.
